summary: This informational RFC describes how responsibilities for the RFC Series are divided among the RFC Series Editor, the RFC Production Center and the RFC Publisher. It also covers IAB oversight through the RFC Series Oversight Committee. It was replaced by RFC 8728.

plainLanguage.summary: A book series needs someone who sets the rules, someone who makes the books, and someone who hands them out. This says who does which job.

questions: what is the rfc editor model
how is the rfc series organized
what does the rfc series editor do
subtitle: Dividing RFC Series responsibilities among three entities

tldr.problem: The RFC Series needed a clear organizational structure with defined responsibilities for editing, production, and publishing RFCs, plus oversight.
tldr.mechanism: The model splits the RFC Editor function into three separate roles: the RFC Series Editor (strategic leadership), the RFC Production Center (editing and processing documents), and the RFC Publisher (distribution and archive).
tldr.outcome: This structure replaced the earlier RFC Editor model (RFC 5620) with clearer role separation and better use of contractors, while the IAB maintains oversight through the RFC Series Oversight Committee.

facts.label: RSE workload
facts.value: approximately 20 hours per week on average

today: RFC 6635 was itself replaced by RFC 8728, which provides an updated model. However, the three-part structure of RSE, Production Center, and Publisher remains the basis for how the RFC Series is organized.

sections.title: The RFC Editor Function
sections.content:
The RFC Series is the permanent record of Internet technical standards and architecture decisions. Originally, a single person called the RFC Editor managed this publication. As the series grew, this work expanded to require multiple people and organizations working together.

RFC 4844 describes the RFC Series as needing an RFC Editor—now understood as a collection of experts and organizations, not a single person. This RFC defines Version 2 of the organizational model, replacing the earlier RFC 5620, based on experience from the first version and community feedback.

The model must balance the IAB's need for quality control and series continuity with the IETF Administrative Oversight Committee's responsibility for cost-effective operations.
sections.plainLanguage: Keeping a series of books going is now too much for one person, so it takes a team. This says how the team is organized.

sections.title: The Three Components
sections.content:
The RFC Editor function is divided into three roles, each with distinct responsibilities:

1. The RFC Series Editor (RSE) is the individual in charge of quality, continuity, and evolution of the RFC Series. Appointed by the IAB but formally hired by the IETF Administrative Oversight Committee (IAOC), the RSE serves as the primary representative of the RFC Series to the Internet community and provides strategic leadership over production and publishing functions. The RSE manages oversight of contractors, determines editorial policies, develops the RFC Series vision, and coordinates cross-stream priorities. The position is expected to consume roughly 20 hours per week on average, with more during IETF meetings.

2. The RFC Production Center is a paid contractor responsible for the detailed editorial work. The Production Center edits documents to comply with the RFC Style Manual, creates records of all edits, identifies potential technical impacts of editorial changes, coordinates with authors and IANA, assigns RFC numbers, and determines when documents are ready for publication. All work is done under the general direction of the RSE but without day-to-day management.

3. The RFC Publisher is a contractor responsible for the operational infrastructure of the RFC Series. The Publisher announces new RFCs, provides online access, manages the errata submission and approval system, performs backups, stores and preserves records, and authenticates RFCs for legal proceedings. Like the Production Center, the Publisher operates under the RSE's general direction.
sections.plainLanguage: One person makes strategy and sets rules; another person edits and checks the text; a third person prints and distributes the books.

sections.title: Governance and Oversight
sections.content:
The RFC Series Oversight Committee (RSOC) acts as the IAB's delegated body for day-to-day oversight of the RFC Series. The RSOC comprises IAB members and outside experts chosen for their Internet community knowledge, IETF expertise, publication experience, and stream-specific knowledge. The IAB appoints an RSOC chair and members who serve at the IAB's pleasure.

The RSOC approves consensus policy and vision documents developed by the RSE and the community, performs annual reviews of the RSE, manages the RSE selection process, ensures transparent and accountable operations, and develops its own rules of order. For decisions affecting the RSE individually (such as hiring and firing), the RSOC prepares recommendations for the IAB, but the IAB retains final authority.

The RSE and the IAOC's liaison serve as non-voting ex officio members of the RSOC. This structure ensures continuity beyond the normal IAB election cycle while protecting the RSE from direct interference by providing a buffer of delegated authority.
sections.plainLanguage: A committee watches the RFC Series Editor and the whole process to make sure everything is fair and transparent.

sections.title: Administrative and Contractual Matters
sections.content:
The IETF Administrative Oversight Committee (IAOC) has ultimate responsibility for implementing the administrative and contractual activities described in the model. The RSE works with the IAOC to define the scope of work (Statement of Work) for contractors and participates in their selection, but the IAOC retains final contracting authority.

The RFC Series portion of the IASA budget includes entries for the RSOC, RSE, RFC Production Center, and RFC Publisher. The RSE must operate within the IAOC-approved budget. If production needs change, the RSE coordinates with the IAOC to determine whether a budgetary adjustment is needed.

When disagreements arise between streams, the RSE, or other RFC Editor entities, the model establishes a clear escalation path. Parties first attempt informal resolution and reconsideration. If that fails, the RSE may decide operational matters to ensure smooth functioning, though the RSE may seek mediation from the IAB Chair. Issues with contractual implications must be brought to the IAOC. Unresolved disagreements may require formal RSOC review and IAB confirmation.
sections.plainLanguage: Money and contracts are managed by an oversight committee, with clear steps for settling disagreements.

sections.title: The RFC Series Editor Role
sections.content:
The RFC Series Editor is expected to be a senior technology professional with significant qualifications. These include strategic leadership and management experience, strong understanding of English and Internet technical terminology, excellent communication skills, and editorial experience. The RSE must understand IETF and RFC processes, work independently, be willing to travel, and be able to function in a complex matrixed environment where authority and responsibility are divided.

The RSE must also have experience with email and teleconference-based collaboration, demonstrated strategic planning and operations management experience, and preferably be an RFC author. Above all, the RSE must avoid any appearance of conflict of interest, such as ownership of or advisory relationships with vendors executing the Production Center or Publisher functions.

The job requires balancing the voices of volunteers in the Internet technical community with the need for clear policy authority. The RSE must consult the community on major policy decisions and work toward consensus while ultimately being able to make final decisions to ensure the RFC Series continues operating smoothly.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC Series Editor needs to be smart, good at communicating, understand the Internet, and be trusted to make fair decisions.
